problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector
examples.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093929/assets/554407e7ec109f5d6e767d87900321d07c253cceefd6e1cdd21ec11351c4548e.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T,
$$

where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

Moreover, $\mathbf u_i\cdot \mathbf u_i^T$ is the projection matrix corresponding to $\mathbf u_i.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac12x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093929/assets/3e365c1786b35c426487c5555bccdb10c67545e5757c8e09b34c514d41ce9219.png)

Therefore, setting $x_2=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093929/assets/e97e23e38548021d0a72c50ff7e34ed108070c482249b23f9cb54a6e812ecc77.png)

where $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093929/assets/23384122e613a5efe2858604b08a1d7353e1b6e08dbc0de4b958a4881a3bda1e.png)

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}15 & -10 \\ -10 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
